Series::index_reduce¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::index_reduce(std::int64_t dim, const Series& index, const Series& source, const std::string& reduce) const
Series Series::index_reduce(std::int64_t dim, const Series& index, const Series& source, const std::string& reduce, bool include_self) const
Series& Series::index_reduce_(std::int64_t dim, const Series& index, const Series& source, const std::string& reduce) const
Series& Series::index_reduce_(std::int64_t dim, const Series& index, const Series& source, const std::string& reduce, bool include_self) const
Series& Series::index_reduce_(std::int64_t dim, const Series& index, const Series& source, const std::string& reduce) const

What It Does¶

Routes source slices to destinations exactly like index_add, but combines repeated destinations with a reduction other than addition: product, mean, maximum, or minimum.

For each source position i, index[i] names a destination slice along dim. Every source slice sent to the same destination forms a group. reduce says how to combine a group; include_self says whether the receiver’s own slice at that destination joins the group as one more member:

result = self.clone()
for destination j named by index:
    group = { self.select(dim, j) } ∪ { source.select(dim, i) : index[i] == j }    -- if include_self
    group =                             { source.select(dim, i) : index[i] == j }    -- otherwise
    result.select(dim, j) = reduce(group)

A destination self never names in index is left completely alone in either mode — include_self = false only removes the receiver from groups that are actually touched, it does not reset the whole tensor to a reduction identity first.

"sum" deliberately has no place here — that accumulation belongs to index_add. index_reduce is the compact way to express “group these routed observations by destination and combine them”, the same job grouped_mean and its siblings do with an explicit group-id tensor instead of a (dim, index) pair.

Reduction Modes¶

  • "prod" multiplies the group’s members.

  • "mean" averages them. With include_self = true the receiver counts as one more contributor at every touched destination. An integral "mean" floors; use a floating dtype when fractional averages matter.

  • "amax" keeps the group’s greatest member.

  • "amin" keeps the group’s smallest member.

Parameters¶

dim (std::int64_t): the axis along which slices are routed. Negative values count from the end.

index (const Series&): a scalar or 1-D int32/int64 series of destination positions along dim, one per source slice. Repeated values form multi-member groups. Values must lie in [0, self.size(dim)) and are not negative-wrapped.

source (const Series&): the slices to reduce. Same rank as self, same size as self on every axis except dim, and the same dtype as self.

reduce (const std::string&): one of "prod", "mean", "amax", or "amin".

include_self (bool, default true): whether the receiver’s own slice joins each touched group as one more member.

Returns¶

Series A new tensor with self’s shape, dtype, and platform. self is untouched. index_reduce_ mutates self in place (preserving its storage) and returns a reference to it.

Gradient¶

Differentiable in both self and source, with a rule specific to each reduce:

  • mean: the upstream sensitivity at a destination is split evenly across every member of that destination’s group (the receiver included, if include_self).

  • amax / amin: sensitivity goes only to the group member(s) that equal the winning value; an exact tie splits it evenly among the tied winners.

  • prod: each nonzero member receives the upstream sensitivity times the product of every other member of its group. A single zero member routes the product of the remaining (nonzero) members to it and zero to everyone else; two or more zero members route zero to every member — a true derivative-of-a-product-through-a-zero case, handled without dividing by zero.

The integer index and the string reduce are non-differentiable.

In-Place Form¶

index_reduce_() is the in-place sibling of index_reduce(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — index_reduce_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 1.0, 1.0}, {3});
auto idx = pluss::series::arange(0, 3, 2, pluss::ScalarType::Int64);
auto src = pluss::make_series({5.0, 7.0}, {2});

x.index_reduce_(0, idx, src, "prod");
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[5, 1, 7]

Examples¶

Example 1. prod with and without the receiver in the group.

auto base = pluss::make_series({10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0});
auto index = pluss::make_series({0, 0, 2});
auto source = pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0, 5.0});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, base.index_reduce(0, index, source, "prod", true));
std::cout << "\n";
pluss::series::print(std::cout, base.index_reduce(0, index, source, "prod", false));

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[60.0000, 20.0000, 150.0000, 40.0000]

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[6.0000, 20.0000, 5.0000, 40.0000]

index = [0, 0, 2] routes source 2 and 3 to destination 0, and source 5 to destination 2. With the receiver included, destination 0 becomes 10*2*3=60; without it, just 2*3=6. Positions 1 and 3 are never named and keep 20 and 40 in both cases — include_self only affects touched groups.

Example 2. mean on the same routing: include_self changes both the numerator and the count.

pluss::series::print(std::cout, base.index_reduce(0, index, source, "mean", true));
std::cout << "\n";
pluss::series::print(std::cout, base.index_reduce(0, index, source, "mean", false));

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[5.0000, 20.0000, 17.5000, 40.0000]

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[2.5000, 20.0000, 5.0000, 40.0000]

The inclusive mean at destination 0 is (10+2+3)/3 = 5; the exclusive mean is (2+3)/2 = 2.5. Destination 2 moves from (30+5)/2 = 17.5 to 5/1 = 5.

Example 3. amax and amin walk the same groups.

pluss::series::print(std::cout, base.index_reduce(0, index, source, "amax", false));
std::cout << "\n";
pluss::series::print(std::cout, base.index_reduce(0, index, source, "amin", true));

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[3.0000, 20.0000, 5.0000, 40.0000]

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[2.0000, 20.0000, 5.0000, 40.0000]

The exclusive maximum at destination 0 compares only 2 and 3, giving 3. The inclusive minimum compares 10, 2, and 3 too, giving 2.

Example 4. dim = 0 on a matrix: whole rows form a group, exactly like index_add’s row-routing, but combined by amax here instead of summed.

auto rows = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 1.0}, {100.0, 100.0}, {1.0, 1.0}});
auto idx = pluss::make_series({0, 0});
auto src = pluss::make_series({{3.0, 5.0}, {7.0, 9.0}});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, rows.index_reduce(0, idx, src, "amax", true));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡   7.0000   9.0000 ⎤
⎢ 100.0000 100.0000 ⎥
⎣   1.0000   1.0000 ⎦

Both source rows route to receiver row 0; per column, the group is {1, 3, 7} and {1, 5, 9}, so row 0 becomes [7, 9]. Rows 1 and 2 were never named and are untouched.

Example 5. Negative dim routes columns instead, using the same rule.

auto cols = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 100.0}, {1.0, 100.0}});
auto idx = pluss::make_series({0, 0});
auto src = pluss::make_series({{3.0, 7.0}, {9.0, 2.0}});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, cols.index_reduce(-1, idx, src, "amax", true));

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ 7.0000 100.0000 ⎤
⎣ 9.0000 100.0000 ⎦

On a 2-D input dim = -1 is dim = 1 (columns). Both source columns route to receiver column 0; column 1 is untouched.

Example 6. Gradient: prod’s reverse multiplies every other member of the group.

auto base = pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0});
auto source = pluss::make_series({4.0, 5.0});
base.tracks_slope_(true);
source.tracks_slope_(true);
base.index_reduce(0, pluss::make_series({0, 0}), source, "prod").sum().reverse();
std::cout << "dbase = "; pluss::series::print(std::cout, base.sensitivity());
std::cout << "dsrc  = "; pluss::series::print(std::cout, source.sensitivity());

Output¶

dbase = Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[20.0000, 1.0000]
dsrc  = Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[10.0000, 8.0000]

Destination 0’s product is 2*4*5=40. The receiver’s local derivative is the product of the other members, 4*5=20; each source member’s is the product of the others (2*5=10 and 2*4=8). Position 1, never named, passes the objective’s sensitivity through untouched as 1.

Example 7. An invalid reduce name fails immediately.

try {
  base.index_reduce(0, pluss::make_series({0, 0}), source, "sum");
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

index_reduce: reduce must be one of 'prod', 'mean', 'amax', or 'amin'

Example 8. A destination outside [0, self.size(dim)) raises.

try {
  auto base = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0});
  auto index = pluss::make_series({7});
  auto source = pluss::make_series({1.0});
  auto y = base.index_reduce(0, index, source, "amax");
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

index_reduce: index value out of range

Example 9. index_reduce_ mutates the receiver in place.

auto base = pluss::make_series({10.0, 20.0, 30.0});
base.index_reduce_(0, pluss::make_series({0, 0}), pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0}), "prod");
pluss::series::print(std::cout, base);

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[60.0000, 20.0000, 30.0000]

index_reduce_’s default include_self = true folds the receiver’s own 10 into the product: 10*2*3 = 60.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • "sum" belongs to index_add and is rejected here.

  • include_self = false changes touched groups only; a destination never named in index is untouched in either mode — it is not reset to a reduction identity.

  • Integral "mean" floors. Use floating self/source for fractional averages.

  • "prod" can overflow fixed-width integer dtypes just like any other product.

  • self and source must match dtype and every non-dim size exactly — the same strict contract as index_add and index_copy.

  • Values inside index are never negative-wrapped, even though dim is.

Summary¶

index_reduce(dim, index, source, reduce, include_self = true) groups source slices by destination and combines each group:

  • routing is identical to index_add; the difference is how repeated destinations combine

  • reduce is "prod", "mean", "amax", or "amin" — never "sum"

  • include_self decides whether the receiver’s own slice joins a touched group; untouched destinations are unaffected either way

  • differentiable, with a reduction-specific backward rule for each mode

See Also¶

  • Series::index_add: the additive sibling — repeated destinations sum instead of reducing.

  • Series::scatter_reduce: the general, full-rank-index form of the same grouped reduction.

  • Series::grouped_mean: group-oriented reduction driven by an explicit group-id tensor rather than a (dim, index) pair.
